Without taking a breath between sentences, your CxO says: “You did a great job automating this process. Where are we going next?”

The reality in most businesses is strong institutional knowledge coupled with process deviation, long change cycles, and siloed views that slow down innovation. You might try to go somewhere next, but it won’t be fast. When a healthcare AI leader shared her journey, attendees started nodding.

Her team received early access to UiPath’s new Cartographer product. They quickly added meeting transcripts, knowledge and training documents, and system documentation to spot gaps in the current process and define the future state. That meant she could pivot the conversation with the business from gaps and documentation to “what we heard,” and even propose several solution design options. For them, the sequence is knowing the information, aligning with partners, engineering and designing the solution, and measuring the impact.
UiPath
Cartographer synthesizes information from multiple documents, specs, process diagrams, architecture blueprints, and artifacts. Several customers shared how it helps them accelerate where in a process to focus and what to ask the business teams, and thereby shorten the time for fact-finding and alignment. It surfaces business rules (incl. timing and approvals), business metrics (durations and delays), and the summary of the pain points mentioned becomes context for new agents.

Finally, to create a holistic process view via the “Map of Work,” Cartographer recommends transformation decisions grounded in the actual business data without having to hunt for details.

We could all use a bit more of that. Yes/ No/ Maybe?

That was the question I kept thinking about at

The theme was accelerating your journey from AI investment to enterprise impact. 
Easy to say. Hard to prove.

Not an AI problem. A process orchestration problem.

From 5 people in a small Bucharest apartment to building one of the world’s leading automation companies. To anyone doubting themselves, may this story inspire you!
Daniel Dines
grew up in Romania and taught himself how to code.

He moved to the US and landed a job at Microsoft, with a stable salary, stock options, and health insurance. For an immigrant, that can feel like the dream.

Then he quit and moved back to Bucharest to start his own company.

𝐇𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐞.
↳ UiPath started with 5 people in a small apartment in Bucharest
 ↳ It took 10 years to raise its first seed round
 ↳ In 2018, it became Romania’s first unicorn
 ↳ In 2021, it listed on the New York Stock Exchange

But one part of Daniel’s story stood out to me: the culture he built.

Early on, he asked his team what allowed 10 engineers from a small country to keep some of the largest enterprises in the world happy.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐡𝐮𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲.

Humility became
UiPath
’s 1rst company value, and the rest grew from there. Today, its 4 values are Humble, Bold, Immersed, and Fast.

Daniel has said that growing up under communism taught him to distrust marketing narratives. Instead, UiPath focused on building great software and trusting customers to recognize its value.

Today, UiPath has grown to more than 3,000 people around the world and is expanding beyond automation into business orchestration, where AI agents, robots, and people work together within governed processes.

If you’re in a tough season right now, let this be your reminder to keep going  💪

Can enterprise AI scale without sacrificing trust?

At
UiPath
FUSION, I spoke with
Andrada Morar
, VP of Customer Experience and Global Partnerships, to explore what it takes to coordinate agents, deterministic automation, systems, and people without losing accountability, context, or trust.

One idea stayed with me:
“Deterministic where you can, agentic where you can’t, humans where you must.” This goes beyond technology architecture. It calls for leadership discipline.

We discussed why process authority must come before automation, how co-innovation with partners is reshaping enterprise AI, why governance must extend across every decision and exception, and why human judgment should remain an intentional design principle.

The conversation also surfaced a more useful way to think about AI. Not as artificial intelligence replacing people, but as individual augmentation that expands what people can accomplish while keeping authority clear.

Watch our conversation and read my full take on
UiPath
’s vision for end-to-end enterprise orchestration at FUSION:

We need to talk about governance. Whether you’re looking to get a grip on agent sprawl in your business or starting to build up your agentic program.

What I heard an AI leader share at
UiPath
FUSION: “Are your agents working safely, accurately, ethically, and are they auditable? Start with the 100th agent in mind! If you start when the 20th agent is in production, you’ll be writing an incident report.” Ouch!

Another point I kept hearing several times from customers: build a “kill-switch” into your agents to stop a runaway agent in the future. Ensure you have a way to roll back an agent’s code to a previous, working state. This approach ensures you don’t put the company at risk of runaway actions or cost, and non-performance.

But when it comes to governance, ensure you agree within the team on the expected return and if the goal is worth pursuing. Help educate the organization on what AI and agents can do realistically and cost-effectively to ground the expectations.

Finally, different levels of impact carry increasing levels of risk (team-, org-, or company-level). Establish agent registries and review processes before agents go live to address it early.

How have you set up your agentic AI governance process?
